title: Abu Dharr
hookLine: plain speaker, critic of hoarded wealth, who walked alone and died alone

lines: A CAMEL THAT CAN'T KEEP UP.
cards: An army is on the march, and one camel can't keep up. It's thin and slow, and its rider falls further behind, until the column is gone over the horizon. So he gets down, loads his things on his own back, and walks.
Later, the people in camp see a figure coming along the road by himself. Someone says: there's a man walking alone. And the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says: let it be Abu Dharr.
It is. Today: Abu Dharr, the man who walked alone.

teach.h: HE WALKS ALONE, HE WILL DIE ALONE.
teach.b: The scene comes from Ibn Ishaq's life of the Prophet, on the road to Tabuk.

When Abu Dharr reaches the camp, tradition says the Prophet spoke of him: may God have mercy on Abu Dharr; he walks alone, he will die alone, and he will be raised alone. Abu Dharr was a man of plain words.
Bukhari keeps a report from late in his life. A visitor found him living out at al-Rabadha, and asked why. In Syria, Abu Dharr explained, he had argued over a verse.
In Pickthall's translation: "They who hoard up gold and silver and spend it not in the way of Allah", followed by a warning of a painful doom. The governor said the verse was about other people.
Abu Dharr said: it's about us and them. The quarrel grew and reached the caliph in Medina, and in the end Abu Dharr settled out at al-Rabadha.

Yet the same Abu Dharr was once corrected. In another report in Bukhari, he insulted a man by mocking his mother, and the Prophet told him plainly: you are a man with the ignorance of the old days still in you.
Later, someone noticed that he and his servant wore matching cloaks, and asked why.
He said the Prophet had taught: your servants are your brothers; feed them from what you eat, dress them from what you wear.
So the plain speaker was corrected too, and he wore the correction, quite literally, on his servant's back.
Tradition says he died at al-Rabadha, far from the city, with his wife beside him, and was buried by travelers who happened by.

how: Muslims remember Abu Dharr al-Ghifari as a companion known for honesty, simple living and concern for the poor, and his reports on treating servants as brothers are taught in lessons on character.

games.q: you're Abu Dharr, on the march, and your camel is too weak to keep up. the army is pulling away. what do you do?
o: wait for someone to come back for you.
load your things on your back and walk.
games.why: he walked on alone, and when he reached the camp the Prophet said: may God have mercy on Abu Dharr; he walks alone.

practice: Bring to mind something true you've been avoiding saying, to a friend, a parent, a manager, or yourself, and find the plainest way to say it in one sentence.

Then dress it with care, the way Abu Dharr dressed his servant in what he wore himself, and say it silently once. If you pray, ask God for courage and gentleness together; if not, just hold the sentence and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Abu Dharr. A companion of plain words, who spoke against hoarded wealth, took correction, and walked alone. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: Abu Dharr, the name by which the companion Jundub ibn Junadah is known.

carryVoice: Your line: walked alone. Plain words, and a servant dressed like himself. Day eight hundred twenty-five, done.
